title: Threads & the Shared-Memory Model
summary: Language-level threading gives you concurrent execution sharing one memory space — and the shared-mutable-state problem every other model in this group exists to avoid. Start here to see the disease before the rest of the group shows the cures.

slides.markdown:
A **thread** is the oldest and most direct concurrency abstraction most languages expose: a second (or third, or thousandth) independent line of execution, running inside the same process, sharing the exact same heap and static state as every other thread.

That sharing is the whole point — and the whole problem. Every other model this group covers (async/await, actors, CSP, structured concurrency) exists at least partly as a reaction to what goes wrong when multiple threads read and write the same mutable memory with no coordination.

This topic is deliberately the "here's the disease" topic before the rest of the group shows different cures. `find the race condition in this multi-threaded counter` is one of the most common live-coding prompts in the industry, and this topic is built to answer it cold.

slides.sectionTitle: What a thread actually gives you
slides.markdown:
A language-level thread gives you exactly one thing: **concurrent execution that shares the same memory space**. Every thread in a process can read and write the same objects, the same static fields, the same everything — there's no copying, no message passing, no isolation by default.

That shared access is cheap to set up (no serialization, no communication protocol — just read the variable) and is exactly why threads remain the lowest-level, most "raw" concurrency primitive most languages expose. Every other model in this group is, in some sense, a layer built on top of threads that restricts or removes this direct sharing, trading some of that rawness for safety.

These two words get used interchangeably and shouldn't be: **concurrency** is about *structure* (multiple tasks making interleaved progress, possibly on one core, taking turns); **parallelism** is about *execution* (multiple tasks literally running at the same instant, which requires multiple cores).

A single-core machine running two threads is concurrent but not parallel — the OS scheduler interleaves them, giving each a slice of time. An eight-core machine running eight threads doing real work simultaneously is both. This distinction matters directly: a CPU-bound task benefits from parallelism (more cores actually doing work), while an I/O-bound task often only needs concurrency (overlapping wait time), which is exactly why `async-await-and-cooperative-concurrency`'s single-threaded model works fine for I/O-heavy workloads.

slides.sectionTitle: Why shared mutable state is the root problem
slides.markdown:
Every concurrency bug class this whole group deals with — races, deadlocks, torn reads, visibility issues — traces back to one root cause: **multiple threads mutating the same memory with no agreed-upon coordination**.

This is worth stating explicitly because the rest of this group is best understood as different answers to the same question: *if shared mutable state is the problem, what do you do instead?* Actors say "never share state, only send messages." CSP says "communicate over explicit channels instead of a shared variable." Lock-free programming says "keep sharing state, but coordinate via atomic hardware operations instead of blocking locks." None of them make concurrency free — they trade the shared-memory model's raw performance for a structural guarantee against a specific bug class.

| Language | Threading API | What it exposes |
|---|---|---|
| Java | `Thread` / `Runnable` | An OS thread wrapped in an object, `start()`/`join()` |
| Python | `threading` module | Same idea, but CPU-bound work is capped by the GIL (`dynamic-language-runtimes-v8-and-cpython`) |
| C++ | `std::thread` | A thin wrapper directly over the OS thread API |

Despite different syntax, all three expose the same underlying concept: an OS-level thread (`process-control-block-and-states`, `thread-implementation-models` in `operating-systems/processes-threads`), created and joined explicitly, sharing memory with every other thread in the process by default. The language-level abstraction barely hides the OS mechanism underneath — this is one of the few concurrency models in this group that's a thin wrapper rather than a genuine language-level construct.

slides.sectionTitle: The fix lives one layer down
slides.markdown:
This topic deliberately stops short of teaching you how to fix the race condition above — mutexes, semaphores, and monitors are OS/language *primitives* that belong to `operating-systems/concurrency-sync` (`locks-and-mutexes`, `monitors-and-condition-variables`, `semaphores`), and this group treats them as a prerequisite, not new material.

What this group covers instead is the *higher-level models* built to reduce how often you need those primitives at all — or to remove the need for them structurally. Knowing both layers is what an interview actually probes: naming `synchronized` or a `Lock` fixes the code sample above, but explaining *why* the actor model or CSP would have prevented the bug from being expressible in the first place is the senior answer.

The pitfall that makes race conditions uniquely painful: they are **non-deterministic**. The exact interleaving of two threads depends on OS scheduling decisions, core count, current system load, and timing — factors that vary run to run, and often vary specifically between a developer's laptop and a production server under load.

This produces the maddening pattern: a race condition passes a hundred local test runs (low contention, few cores, lucky timing) and then fails in production under real concurrent load, or worse, fails intermittently and vanishes the moment you attach a debugger — because the debugger's pauses change the timing enough to avoid the bad interleaving. This is why race conditions can't be reliably caught by "just run the tests more" — they need either careful code review for shared-mutable-state access, or tools specifically built to detect races (thread sanitizers, stress-testing frameworks that deliberately vary scheduling).

slides.sectionTitle: Where this group goes from here
slides.markdown:
With the shared-memory model's core problem established, the rest of this group shows genuinely different structural answers:

- **`async-await-and-cooperative-concurrency`** — one thread, no sharing problem across threads at all, cooperative switching instead of preemption.
- **`the-actor-model`** and **`csp-and-channels`** — no shared state by construction; communicate via messages or channels instead.
- **`lock-free-programming-and-stm`** — keep sharing state, but coordinate through atomic hardware primitives instead of blocking locks.
- **`structured-concurrency`** — a discipline for scoping concurrent work so it can't outlive its logical owner, regardless of which underlying model you're using.

`comparing-concurrency-models` closes the group by putting all of these side by side against the same design question this topic opened with.
